transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, um... thank you. Well, I guess I'm here because... things are just really, really hard at work right now, and it's starting to become a huge problem. I work retail, just at this clothing shop downtown, and it's usually fine, I've been there a while, but... well, I came in because I just, I literally can’t make myself go near the front windows anymore. Or even that part of the street outside. 

It's like, I have to walk a whole block out of my way before my shift just to get to the back alley entrance, because if I go near the front doors or that stretch of the sidewalk, I just... I can't. And inside the store, the windows are huge, you know, they're those big floor-to-ceiling glass ones for the displays, and I just can't be anywhere near them. I keep finding all these ridiculous excuses to stay in the back stockroom. Like, I'll tell my manager I need to recount the accessories inventory, or steam a whole rack of new shipments, or break down all the cardboard boxes—just anything, absolutely anything, so I don't have to go out on the main floor. Which is really bad, because being out there with the customers is literally my whole job. I'm a salesperson, I'm supposed to be out there greeting people and fixing the displays, but I just hide in the back room all day because I can't even look toward the front of the store without feeling like I'm going to lose my mind.
Is there something specific that you're afraid of when you're near the front windows or that part of the street outside?

Well, it's... it's not exactly that I'm afraid of something new happening, it's more like... I'm afraid of what's already happened, if that makes sense? Because, well, there was this awful crash, and it just... it keeps popping into my head, completely out of nowhere. I'll be trying to do something totally normal, like, I don't know, trying to set up a new display of sweaters or arranging the mannequins, trying to force myself to be out there on the floor, and then suddenly, it's just right there. 

It's like I'm not even in the store anymore, I'm right back in that exact moment. I can hear this deafening bang, just this horrible, crunching metal sound, and then... and then I see the glass. The whole front window just coming down, shattering everywhere, all these huge, sharp pieces flying in. It's so real, it's like it's happening all over again right in front of me. I can almost feel the wind and the dust hitting my face. And it just plays on a loop in my head, over and over, no matter how hard I try to push it away or focus on my work. It's just so exhausting, having to relive it like that, especially when I'm just trying to fold some shirts or something. It just takes over everything.
Do you ever have episodes where you feel an intense fear or discomfort that reaches a peak within minutes, with symptoms like a racing heart or shortness of breath?

Um... no, not exactly like that. I mean, my heart definitely beats really fast when I get those flashes, like when I see the glass breaking in my head again, and I definitely feel panicked then. But it's not like... it's not like it just comes out of nowhere and peaks like you're saying, like a sudden attack of just pure fear for no reason. 

It's always tied to the crash, or thinking about the crash, or being near the front of the store. Like, if I'm back in the stockroom, just unpacking boxes and totally distracted, I don't suddenly get this wave of terror where I can't breathe. It's only when my brain goes back to that moment. So, I don't think I have those... whatever you'd call them, those sudden episodes you're describing. It's more just a constant dread of having to see the windows, and then the actual panic when the memory forces its way in. But not just random attacks of my heart racing, no.
Do you try to avoid thinking about the crash or talking about it with others?

Well, I... I guess I do try to avoid it, yeah. I mean, I really try to just push it out of my head whenever it starts creeping in, because if I let myself think about it for even a second, it's like opening the floodgates and I'm right back there with the glass and the noise. So if I feel my mind wandering toward that day, I'll immediately try to distract myself. Like, I'll start counting the hangers on a rack, or I'll try to recite the lyrics to a song, just anything to keep my brain occupied so it doesn't go there. 

And as for talking about it... I really, really don't want to. My mom keeps calling and asking how I'm doing, if I'm "processing" things, and I just change the subject. I tell her about the new fall inventory or complain about a rude customer, just completely pivoting away from the crash. Even my coworkers, the ones who weren't working that shift, they try to ask me what happened, like they want all the gory details, and I just... I make up an excuse to go to the bathroom or the stockroom. I just can't talk about it. It's like, if I say the words out loud, it makes it real all over again, and I just can't handle that right now. I just want to pretend it didn't happen, even though I know that's probably not healthy, but talking about it just makes my chest feel tight and I start getting all shaky. So yeah, I definitely avoid thinking or talking about it as much as humanly possible.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings and reactions to the crash?

Well, it feels like it's been a lifetime, honestly, but it's really only been about two weeks. Yeah, two weeks exactly this coming Thursday. That was the night of the overnight shift, the inventory shift we do once a quarter where we stay until like 3:00 AM counting everything. I usually don't even mind those shifts because it's quiet and we can play our own music over the speakers, you know? But that night... that's when it happened. That's when the car just came completely through the front window. 

So yeah, ever since that exact night, it's been like this. Two weeks of just... constant on-edge feeling, the flashes, the trying not to think about it. It started almost immediately after, like the very next day when I tried to go to sleep and I just couldn't because every time I closed my eyes, I saw the headlights. And it hasn't let up since. Every single day for the last fourteen days, it's just been this exhausting cycle. I keep hoping I'll wake up and it'll be a little bit better, that maybe a week out it would fade, or two weeks out, but here we are at two weeks and it still feels just as fresh and just as terrifying as it did the moment it actually happened.
Do you ever feel like you're detached from yourself or the world around you when you're experiencing these flashbacks or trying to avoid thinking about the crash?

Um... yeah, actually. That happens a lot, especially when I'm just trying to get through a shift. It's the weirdest feeling, like... like I'm not really there? I don't know how to explain it perfectly, but sometimes I'll be out on the sales floor, right? Just folding sweaters or organizing the clearance rack, trying so hard not to look at the front windows, and suddenly everything just feels... off. 

The fluorescent lights overhead, the racks of clothes, the mannequins... they all start to feel really far away. And fake, almost? Like I'm walking around on a movie set instead of the actual store I've worked in for three years. It's like the volume on the world gets turned down, and the colors get a little washed out. And then I get this sensation like I'm... I'm watching myself do things. Like I'm floating just behind my own shoulder, watching my hands fold a shirt, but I don't actually feel my hands touching the fabric. I'm just observing this girl in a name tag moving through the aisles. 

It happened just yesterday. A customer asked me where the fitting rooms were, and I heard my voice answer her, gave her the exact directions, but it didn't feel like *I* was talking. It felt like I was watching someone else use my voice. It's really unsettling, honestly, because I know I'm there, I know I'm at work, but my brain just sort of disconnects from my body. I'll just stand there for a minute, blinking, trying to force myself to feel the ground under my shoes just to snap back into reality. But yeah, it just feels like the whole world is made of cardboard and I'm just a ghost haunting the women's department. It usually happens right when I'm fighting off a memory of the crash, like my brain just pulls the plug to keep me from panicking, but then I'm just stuck in this weird, floaty, fake version of the store.
Do you feel guilty about what happened during the crash?

Guilty? I... no, I don't think so. I mean, I don't feel guilty, exactly. It's more just... I don't know, it was just so random, you know? Like, we were just doing inventory. I was standing by the cash wrap, holding a scanner, and then suddenly there's a car in the store. I didn't cause it, obviously, and I couldn't have stopped it. It's not like I was the one driving the car or anything. 

But I do think about it a lot, just... the sequence of events. Like, if I had been standing two feet to the left, I would have been right where the bumper hit the display table. Or if I had gone to the breakroom to grab a water bottle when I was thinking about it five minutes earlier, I wouldn't have even been in the front of the store. It's just so crazy how fast it happened, and I keep replaying it, but no, I don't feel guilty. I just feel... terrified, mostly. And overwhelmed. But not guilty. It was just a freak accident, and I just happened to be there, trying to scan a stack of denim.
Are there any activities or tasks outside of work that you've stopped doing or are avoiding because of what happened during the crash?

Um... outside of work? No, not really. I mean, I guess I haven't really thought about it like that, because work is the main thing, you know? That's where it happened. So that's where I'm having the hardest time. Like, I haven't stopped going to the grocery store or anything. I still go to Trader Joe's on Sunday mornings like I always do, because I have to get my groceries for the week, and I still go to the laundromat on Tuesday nights because my apartment building doesn't have machines. 

I guess... I mean, I haven't been going out with my friends as much, but that's not because I'm avoiding the places we go. It's not like I'm scared to go to the diner or the movies. It's just that I'm so exhausted from dealing with the flashbacks and the floaty feelings at work that by the time I get home, I just want to curl up in a ball on my couch and watch TV until I pass out. I just don't have the energy to socialize. But it's not like I'm actively avoiding, like, driving or walking down certain streets or anything like that. 

I did think about not going to my sister's birthday dinner last weekend because it was at a restaurant on a busy corner, and for a second I was like, 'What if a car comes through that window?' But I went anyway. I just made sure I sat facing the door, on the inside of the booth, as far away from the glass as possible. So I'm still doing things, I'm just... doing them differently, I guess? But yeah, no, I haven't completely stopped doing anything outside of the store. It's really just the store itself that's the huge problem.
Do you have any trouble remembering parts of what happened during the crash?

Trouble remembering? God, I wish. No, I... I remember every single second of it. It's actually the exact opposite of not remembering. It's like... it's burned into my brain in high definition. I can tell you exactly what was happening right before, during, and after, down to the tiniest, most stupid details. 

Like I said, I was standing by the cash wrap with the inventory scanner, and I was scanning this stack of straight-leg denim, the light wash ones that we just got in for the spring floor set. And the store radio was playing that one really annoying pop song—I think it was a Dua Lipa song, just standard retail background music, right? And I was thinking about how much my feet hurt because I wore my new boots instead of sneakers. 

And then there was this... this screeching sound, like tires, but it sounded so out of place inside a mall, you know? And then just the loudest crash I've ever heard in my entire life. I remember the exact way the glass from the front windows just sort of... exploded inward. It didn't just break, it shattered into a million tiny little pieces flying through the air, and I remember watching the mannequins in the front window display just getting absolutely obliterated by the hood of this silver sedan. 

And the smell! I remember the smell so vividly, which is weird because you don't think about smells during something like that. But it was this awful mix of burnt rubber, exhaust fumes, and all the weird, chalky dust that got kicked up from the drywall and the ceiling tiles falling down. I remember the sound of the metal clothing racks screeching and scraping against the floor tiles as the car pushed them back into the aisles. I even remember the driver's face, just looking completely stunned behind the windshield, gripping the steering wheel. 

So, yeah, no gaps at all. I honestly wish my brain would just delete some of those files, you know? Because I remember every single agonizing detail of it. It just plays on a loop in my head. So no, no trouble remembering anything. If anything, I remember way too much of it.
Do you find yourself being constantly on the lookout for potential dangers or threats, even when you're not at work?

I mean, constantly on the lookout? I... I don't know if I'd call it constantly, exactly. Like, I'm not walking down the street checking over my shoulder every two seconds or, like, peering around corners before I turn them. It's not like I'm living in an action movie or something. 

But I guess... I mean, like I said about my sister's birthday dinner, I definitely pay more attention to things now. Like, where the exits are, or how close I am to the street if I'm walking on the sidewalk. Or if I'm at the grocery store, I'll catch myself looking at the big glass automatic doors and just sort of... wondering. But it's not this intense, overwhelming feeling of being hunted, you know? It's just a fleeting thought, like my brain is just doing a quick safety check. 

I don't feel like I'm constantly on edge everywhere I go. It's really just... it's just the store. That's where I feel like I have to be on guard, because that's where the bad thing actually happened. Outside of work, I'm mostly just tired. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm constantly on the lookout for danger everywhere else. Just... maybe a little more aware of my surroundings than I used to be? But not in a crazy, paranoid way. Just normal aware.
Have you been having trouble sleeping since the crash?

Trouble sleeping? Honestly, no. I really haven't had any trouble sleeping at all. I know that sounds weird, considering everything else that's going on, but sleep is actually the one thing that hasn't been a problem. 

Like I said earlier, I'm just so exhausted by the time I get home from work. It's like my brain has been running a marathon all day, dealing with the flashbacks and trying to act normal while feeling completely detached from reality. So by the time I actually get into bed, I'm practically dead on my feet. I usually just crash immediately. 

I don't lie awake staring at the ceiling or tossing and turning or anything like that. I usually put on this sleep playlist I have—it's mostly just ambient noise, like rain sounds and low-fi beats, because total silence is a little too quiet for me anyway, even before the crash. But yeah, once I close my eyes, I'm out. I sleep straight through the night, usually until my alarm goes off at 7:00 AM. 

I mean, sometimes I wake up feeling like I haven't slept, like I'm still tired, but the actual act of falling asleep and staying asleep? No issues there. It's actually kind of a relief, to be honest. It's the one part of my day where my brain finally just... shuts off, you know? Where I don't have to think about the store or the car or the noise. So yeah, thankfully, my sleep has been completely fine. I don't know what I'd do if I was dealing with all of this *and* I couldn't sleep on top of it. That would just be too much.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with friends or family since the crash?

Changes in my relationships? Um... no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed anything different. I guess I'm still talking to everyone the same amount. Like, my mom still calls me every other day to check in, and we talk about normal stuff, you know? She tells me about her garden or what my dad is complaining about that week. And my friends... well, we have this big group chat on iMessage, and it's still going off all day with TikTok links and memes and people complaining about their jobs. I still chime in when I can. 

I guess I did go to my sister's birthday dinner last week, like I mentioned earlier, and that was totally fine. I mean, I was a little distracted by the seating arrangement and the exits, like I said, but the actual interacting with my family part? That was completely normal. We had Italian food, and my brother made his usual stupid jokes, and I laughed and talked just like I always do. It's not like I'm shutting people out or ignoring their texts or anything. 

I think because I feel so weird and disconnected at work, I actually try to make sure I'm acting as normal as possible with my friends and family. I don't want them to worry, you know? So if they ask how I am, I just say I'm fine, just tired from work, which isn't a total lie. I just leave out the part about feeling like I'm floating outside my body half the day. But yeah, no fights, no pulling away, no drama. Everything with them is pretty much exactly the same as it was before the car crashed into the store. I'm just... trying to keep that part of my life normal, even if the rest of it feels completely messed up. So, no, no changes there.
Have you felt like your symptoms have significantly interfered with your ability to function or enjoy daily life outside of work?

Well, outside of work... no, not really. Like I said, I'm still talking to my friends and going to family dinners and all that. It's really just work where everything feels like it's falling apart. 

I mean, I don't know if I mentioned this, but the other day my manager asked me to do a window reset. Which is totally normal, right? We change the front displays all the time. But I was out there, right by the big glass windows at the front of the store, and... I just couldn't do it. I was trying to dress the mannequins and arrange the new stock, but my hands were shaking, and I kept looking out at the parking lot, just waiting for another car to come crashing through. It was like I could hear the glass breaking all over again, even though it was completely quiet. 

I tried to push through it, I really did. I kept telling myself I was being ridiculous, that it was just a window display, but my heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out. I ended up just dropping a stack of folded sweaters right there on the floor and walking away in the middle of it. I had to go hide in the stockroom for like twenty minutes just to catch my breath. 

My manager was pretty annoyed, obviously, because I just abandoned the project half-finished, and I had to make up some excuse about feeling sick. But honestly, now I'm just... I'm terrified. I'm so worried that I can't handle any part of my job that involves being near the storefront. And in retail, you're always near the storefront! You have to greet customers, you have to fix displays, you have to stand at the registers... and if I can't even do a basic window reset without having a total meltdown, how am I supposed to keep working there? It's just... it's really messing with my ability to actually do my job, you know? But outside of work, at home or with my family? No, I think I'm functioning okay there. It's just the store. It's always just the store.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Lost interest? Um, I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, I still like the same stuff I always liked. Like, I still watch my shows. Every Thursday night I watch that new reality dating show with my roommate, and we still order Thai food and make fun of the contestants, just like we did before. And I still like going to the park on Sundays to read, although I guess I haven't done that the last couple of weekends just because it's been raining, not because I didn't want to. 

And I still really like doing my makeup in the mornings. That's always been my favorite part of getting ready, just putting on a podcast and taking my time blending my eyeshadow. I even bought a new palette last week online, one of those really pretty neutral ones with the shimmers that I've been wanting for months. So I'm still excited about things like that. 

I guess... I mean, I'm definitely more tired, like I said, so maybe I don't have the energy to do as *much* as I used to. Like, if my friends want to go out on a Friday night to a crowded bar, I might pass on that right now just because I'm so drained from holding it together at the store all week. But it's not that I don't *want* to go or that I don't think it would be fun, I just physically feel like I need to be on my couch in my sweatpants instead. So the interest is still there, definitely. I still want to do all my normal things. It's just the energy part that's a little lacking right now. But yeah, no, I wouldn't say I've lost interest in my hobbies or anything like that. I'm still me, you know? Just... a really exhausted version of me.
Do you find yourself being easily startled by loud noises or unexpected movements?

Oh my gosh, yes. Yes, completely. It's actually really embarrassing because I feel like I'm constantly jumping out of my skin over every little thing. Like, it doesn't even have to be that loud, it just has to be sudden, you know? 

Like yesterday, I was in the break room at work—which is usually the only place I feel somewhat okay, because there are no windows and it's in the back—and one of my coworkers, Sarah, she came in and just sort of let the door swing shut behind her. And it wasn't even a slam, it was just a normal click, but I literally gasped and dropped my phone on the floor. My whole body just jerked. And Sarah was looking at me like I was crazy, and I had to laugh it off and say I was just daydreaming, but my heart was pounding so fast I could feel it in my throat for like ten minutes afterward. 

And it's not just at work, either. If I'm walking to my apartment and a car honks out on the street—even if it's a couple of blocks away—I just freeze, and my shoulders shoot up to my ears. Or if someone comes up behind me when I don't hear them... like, my roommate was in the kitchen the other night, and I didn't realize she was home, and she just said "Hey" from behind me while I was getting a glass of water. I jumped so hard I spilled water all over the counter and down my shirt. And then I started crying, which was so stupid, but I just couldn't get my heart to slow down. 

Even the delivery carts at the mall... you know those big metal ones they use to bring boxes from the loading dock? If one of those bangs against a door frame or rattles over the tile floor, it's like an electric shock goes right through me. I just instantly tense up, and I'm looking around wildly like something terrible is about to happen. It's so exhausting, honestly, because I feel like I'm just constantly waiting for the next loud noise to happen so I can overreact to it. I never used to be jumpy like this at all. I used to be the person who wouldn't even wake up during a thunderstorm, and now a car horn two streets over makes me feel like I'm having a heart attack.
Have you been experiencing any physical symptoms like headaches or stomach problems since the crash?

Headaches or stomach problems? Um... no, actually. Not really. I mean, I did think I was getting a headache the other day, like right behind my eyes, you know that kind of dull ache? But then I realized I just hadn't drank any water for my entire shift because I was too anxious to walk past the front windows to get to the break room where the water cooler is. So it was probably just dehydration, because the second I got back to my apartment and chugged a huge glass of ice water, it went away completely. I actually used to get headaches a lot from the fluorescent lights in the store, they buzz and they're just so bright, but since the crash, I've been keeping my head down a lot and just looking at the floor or the clothing racks when I have to be out there, so the lights haven't even been bothering me as much, ironically. 

And as for my stomach... no, my stomach has been totally fine. Like I mentioned earlier, I'm still eating normally. My roommate and I had that Thai food on Thursday, and we always get the super spicy drunken noodles, which sometimes makes me a little bloated if I eat it too late at night, but honestly, I digested it perfectly fine this week. I don't feel nauseous or sick to my stomach or anything like that. 

I guess the only physical stuff I'm really dealing with is just what I was saying before, you know, the heart pounding and the shaking and just feeling so completely drained and heavy all the time. But as far as actual pain, like a bad migraine or an upset stomach, no, I haven't really had anything like that pop up. I've always had a pretty iron stomach anyway. Even when I was a kid in elementary school, I never really got those stomach bugs when everyone else in my class was out sick for a week. My mom always said I had an immune system made of steel. So yeah, thankfully no stomach issues, because having to run to the bathroom feeling sick while I'm already freaking out about just being near the storefront would just be a total nightmare. So, no, just the jumpiness and the exhaustion, really. No headaches or anything.
Are there any specific places or situations outside of work that you avoid because they remind you of the crash?

Outside of work? Um, well, mostly it's just that specific part of the street where it happened. Like, I will absolutely not go anywhere near that stretch of the road anymore. I used to walk down that way all the time, you know, to grab a coffee at the little corner cafe before my shift, or just to get to my usual bus stop, but now I will literally map out these ridiculous detours on my phone and walk like four or five blocks out of my way just so I don't have to even see that intersection. I can't even look in that direction if I'm walking a street over. 

But honestly, it's not just outside of work, it's everything connected to it, which is actually the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I came in because I just can't make myself go near the front windows of the store anymore, or that part of the street outside, like I said. It's gotten to the point where I keep finding all these ridiculous excuses to stay in the back room. I'll tell my manager I need to reorganize the overstock, or I'll offer to sweep the back hallway, or I'll just sort the plastic hangers by size for an hour—literally anything to keep me away from the front of the shop. 

And it's becoming a really big problem because being out on the sales floor and greeting people by the entrance is, you know, a huge part of my job. I'm supposed to be out there doing the window displays and helping customers as soon as they walk in. But the second I even think about walking up to those big glass windows, my chest gets all tight and I just picture it happening all over again, so I just turn around and hide in the back. My manager is definitely starting to notice that I'm never on the floor, but I just don't know how to explain it to her. So yeah, avoiding that street and those windows is basically ruling my life right now.
Are there any other specific situations or places outside of work that you try to avoid because they remind you of the crash?

Um, honestly, I know I kind of just dumped all that on you a second ago, but no, there really aren't any other places besides what I just mentioned. It’s exactly like I was just saying—that’s the entire reason I finally caved and came in to see you today. I came in because I literally cannot make myself go near those front windows at the shop, or walk down that specific part of the street anymore. It’s like there’s a physical, invisible wall stopping me. 

And, you know, I just keep finding all these dumb excuses to stay in the back room at work, even though being out on the floor is my actual job. I'm not avoiding, like, the grocery store, or the movie theater, or my gym or anything like that... it's really just that one specific area. But because my job is right there, it's becoming this huge, unmanageable issue. I'll literally volunteer to scrub the breakroom microwave or take out the heavy trash bags just so my manager doesn't ask me to go restock the mannequins by the glass. It's so embarrassing having to dodge my own job duties like that, and I know I sound like a broken record, but I just absolutely cannot go near the front. So, yeah, no other places really, just... just that street and the storefront.

patient.answer:

It’s exactly like I was just saying—that’s the entire reason I finally caved and came in to see you today. I came in because I literally cannot make myself go near those front windows at the shop, or walk down that specific part of the street anymore. It’s like there’s a physical, invisible wall stopping me. 

And, you know, I just keep finding all these dumb excuses to stay in the back room at work, even though being out on the floor is my actual job. I'm not avoiding, like, the grocery store, or the movie theater, or my gym or anything like that... it's really just that one specific area. But because my job is right there, it's becoming this huge, unmanageable issue. I'll literally volunteer to scrub the breakroom microwave or take out the heavy trash bags just so my manager doesn't ask me to go restock the mannequins by the glass. It's so embarrassing having to dodge my own job duties like that, and I know I sound like a broken record, but I just absolutely cannot go near the front. So, yeah, no other places really, just... just that street and the storefront.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including flashbacks, avoidance of triggers that remind them of the crash, and significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning, are consistent with Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The patient's experience of a traumatic event, the car crash into the store, and their subsequent reactions to it, such as intense fear, helplessness, or horror, also support this diagnosis.
